rows.first: Is a former President immune from criminal prosecution for his official acts?

shown.text: Jackson, J., dissenting: “It holds that a former President may or may not be immune from criminal prosecution for conduct undertaken while in office, to be determined on a case-by-case basis.”

Jackson, J., dissenting: “First, with respect to any criminal conduct relating to a President’s “core constitutional powers”—those subjects “within his ‘conclusive and preclusive’ constitutional authority”—the President is entitled to absolute immunity from criminal prosecution.”

Jackson, J., dissenting: “Second, expanding outward from this “core,” regarding all other “acts within the outer perimeter of [the President’s] official responsibility,” the President is entitled to “at least a presumptive immunity from criminal prosecution.””

Opinion of the Court (Roberts): “We granted certiorari to consider the following question: “Whether and if so to what extent does a former President enjoy presidential immunity from criminal prosecution for conduct alleged to involve official acts during his tenure in office.””
Opinion of the Court (Roberts): “The parties before us do not dispute that a former President can be subject to criminal prosecution for unofficial acts committed while in office.”
Opinion of the Court (Roberts): “They disagree, however, about whether a former President can be prosecuted for his official actions.”

Opinion of the Court (Roberts): “We conclude that under our constitutional structure of separated powers, the nature of Presidential power requires that a former President have some immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts during his tenure in office.”
Opinion of the Court (Roberts): “At least with respect to the President’s exercise of his core constitutional powers, this immunity must be absolute.”

removed.text: The majority’s indecision as to “whether [official-acts] immunity must be absolute” or whether, instead, “presumptive immunity is sufficient,” ... hardly matters.

rows.first: Does Title VII protect gay and transgender employees from being fired?

shown.text: Opinion of the Court (Gorsuch): “If an employer would not have discharged an employee but for that individual’s sex, the statute’s causation standard is met, and liability may attach.”

Opinion of the Court (Gorsuch): “No less, intentional discrimination based on sex violates Title VII, even if it is intended only as a means to achieving the employer’s ultimate goal of discriminating against homosexual or transgender employees.”

Syllabus: “An employer who intentionally fires an individual homosexual or transgender employee in part because of that individual’s sex violates the law even if the employer is willing to subject all male and female homosexual or transgender employees to the same rule.”
Syllabus: “Nor is it a defense to insist that intentional discrimination based on homosexuality or transgender status is not intentional discrimination based on sex.”
Opinion of the Court (Gorsuch): “But these conversational conventions do not control Title VII’s legal analysis, which asks simply whether sex was a but-for cause.”
Syllabus: “Held: An employer who fires an individual merely for being gay or transgender violates Title VII.”
Alito, J., dissenting: “Title VII prohibits discrimination based on five specified grounds, and neither sexual orientation nor gender identity is on the list.”
Opinion of the Court (Gorsuch): “the employer intentionally singles out an employee to fire based in part on the employee’s sex, and the affected employee’s sex is a but-for cause of his discharge.”

shown.text: Sotomayor, J., dissenting: “In the end, when the Court speaks of a “colorblind” Constitution, it cannot really mean it, for it is faced with a body of law that recognizes that race-conscious measures are permissible under the Equal Protection Clause.”
Sotomayor, J., dissenting: “Overruling decades of precedent, today's newly constituted Court singles out the limited use of race in holistic college admissions.”
Sotomayor, J., dissenting: “At bottom, without any new factual or legal justification, the Court overrides its longstanding holding that diversity in higher education is of compelling value.”
Sotomayor, J., dissenting: “The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment enshrines a guarantee of racial equality.”
Sotomayor, J., dissenting: “The Court long ago concluded that this guarantee can be enforced through race-conscious means in a society that is not, and has never been, colorblind.”

Sotomayor, J., dissenting: “For 45 years, the Court extended Brown's transformative legacy to the context of higher education, allowing colleges and universities to consider race in a limited way and for the limited purpose of promoting the important benefits of racial diversity.”
